choices: Mount a Windows 11 ISO matching the installed build and rerun DISM /RestoreHealth with /Source pointing at the install.wim
Run SFC /scannow repeatedly until it reports no errors
Disable Windows Update and deploy updates with a third-party patching agent instead
Reset all affected PCs with 'keep my files' to rebuild the OS
desc: Repair a corrupted Windows component store blocking cumulative updates.
evidence:
Error: 0x800f081f
The source files could not be found.
Use the "Source" option to specify the location of the files that are required to restore the feature.
Failed to resolve package for servicing ... HRESULT = 0x800f081f - CBS_E_SOURCE_MISSING
Windows Resource Protection found corrupt files but was unable to fix some of them.
hint: The error literally says the source files could not be found — the repair tool needs somewhere to get good copies from.
objectives: Interpret the 0x800f081f error code
Repair the component store with DISM using a known-good source
Verify the repair before retrying the update
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A fleet of Windows 11 workstations fails the monthly cumulative update with error 0x800f081f. Running SFC /scannow reports it found corrupt files but could not repair some of them. The failures began after an interrupted feature update on several machines.
title: The Update That Would Not Install
why: 0x800f081f (CBS_E_SOURCE_MISSING) means DISM cannot find healthy replacement files in the local component store or via Windows Update. Pointing DISM at a mounted ISO's install.wim with /Source gives it a known-good payload. Repeating SFC cannot work because SFC draws from the same broken store; disabling updates or resetting PCs are disproportionate and destructive compared to a targeted repair.

choices: Stop the spooler, delete the files in the PRINTERS folder, remove the suspect driver package, then restart the service
Change the spooler startup type to Automatic (Delayed Start) so it recovers on its own
Reinstall the printer with the same driver version that is already installed
Disable the Print Spooler service on the workstation as a precaution
desc: Break a repeating Print Spooler crash caused by a corrupt job and bad driver.
evidence: The Print Spooler service terminated unexpectedly. It has done this 5 time(s). The following corrective action will be taken in 60000 milliseconds: Restart the service.
Event Viewer > Application log, spoolsv.exe crash

Faulting application name: spoolsv.exe
Faulting module name: P6PRINT.DLL (a third-party PCL6 driver module)
Exception code: 0xc0000005
hint: The crash repeats because the spooler re-reads the same corrupt job and loads the same bad driver every time it starts.
objectives: Correlate the service crash pattern in Event Viewer
Clear the stuck spool files safely
Remove the faulty driver package causing the crash
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A shared front-desk workstation cannot print. The Print Spooler service starts and then stops again within a minute, every time. Restarting the service manually produces the same result, and the print queue never clears.
title: Print Spooler Crash Loop
why: The evidence points at a corrupt spool file plus a faulting third-party driver module. Stopping the service, clearing the PRINTERS folder, and removing the driver package breaks the crash loop at its root. Delayed Start only delays the crash; reinstalling the same driver reintroduces the fault; disabling the service 'fixes' printing by removing printing.

choices: Add the Berlin branch computers to the Berlin-Workstations group used in the GPO's security filtering
Move the Berlin computers into a new OU and link a copy of the GPO there
Enable loopback processing on the GPO
Run gpupdate /force /boot on every Berlin workstation
desc: Diagnose a drive-mapping GPO denied by security filtering.
evidence:
The following GPOs were not applied because they were filtered out
-------------------------------------------------------------------
    Drive Maps - Berlin
        Filtering: Denied (Security)

Trustee: Berlin-Workstations | Permission: GpoApply
Trustee: Authenticated Users | Permission: (removed)
MemberOf: (empty - the computer is not in Berlin-Workstations)
hint: 'Denied (Security)' means the computer was never in the GPO's audience — check who the GPO applies to.
objectives: Use gpresult to identify why a GPO is filtered out
Inspect the GPO's security filtering
Verify computer group membership
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A new drive-mapping GPO linked to the Workstations OU is not applying to computers at the Berlin branch office. gpupdate /force completes with no errors, but the mapped drive never appears. Other GPOs linked to the same OU apply to those computers normally.
title: GPO Filtered Out by Security
why: gpresult says the denial is security filtering, and the permissions show only Berlin-Workstations gets GpoApply while the computer is not a member. Adding the computers to that group puts them in scope. A new OU, loopback, or forced refresh cannot help because the computer is filtered out before any settings are even considered.

choices: Correct DHCP option 006 on the 10.20.30.0 scope to the real DNS servers, then renew client leases
Add a hosts file entry for intranet on every affected workstation
Reboot the DHCP server to clear its cache
Switch the affected workstations to static IPs with the correct DNS servers
desc: Trace a DNS failure to a misconfigured DHCP scope option.
hint: 192.0.2.53 is in a documentation range — it can never answer queries. Where did the clients learn that address?
objectives: Confirm the failure is DNS, not general connectivity
Identify the misconfigured DHCP option
Correct the scope and refresh client leases
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: Every workstation on the 10.20.30.0/24 subnet lost name resolution this morning: intranet sites, file shares by name, and email autodiscover all fail, but everything works by IP address. Other subnets are unaffected. The DHCP server was 'tidied up' by a junior admin yesterday.
title: Subnet Loses Name Resolution
why: Clients reach everything by IP but not by name, and every affected client points at an unroutable documentation-range DNS address handed out by DHCP option 006. Fixing the scope option repairs all current and future leases at the source. Hosts-file edits and static IPs are unscalable band-aids, and rebooting the DHCP server changes nothing about the wrong option value.

choices: Find the device holding the statically assigned duplicate (MAC 8C-3B-4A-11-22-33), give it a free address or a DHCP reservation, and document it
Increase the DHCP lease duration so addresses stop changing
Replace the printer's network cable
Add a second IP address to the printer so it can answer on either
desc: Diagnose intermittent drops caused by a duplicate IP address.
evidence:
Reply from 10.20.40.25: bytes=32 time=2ms TTL=64
Request timed out.
Reply from 10.20.40.25: bytes=32 time=41ms TTL=64
Request timed out.
The system detected an address conflict for IP address 10.20.40.25 with the system having network hardware address 8C-3B-4A-11-22-33.

First check:  10.20.40.25  8c-3b-4a-11-22-33  dynamic
Second check: 10.20.40.25  00-1e-0b-aa-bb-cc  dynamic
hint: The ARP entry for one IP keeps flipping between two MAC addresses — two devices are answering for the same address.
objectives: Recognize the intermittent pattern of an IP conflict
Confirm the conflict in logs and ARP data
Locate the offending device and resolve the duplication
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A network printer at 10.20.40.25 drops off the network intermittently: print jobs stall, then suddenly resume, in no pattern. The printer's link light stays on, and a continuous ping alternates between replies and timeouts.
title: The Phantom Printer Outage
why: Flapping ARP entries plus the Tcpip address-conflict event prove two devices claim 10.20.40.25 — typically a statically configured device colliding with a DHCP assignment. Re-addressing the offender (ideally via a reservation) ends the conflict permanently. Lease duration, cabling, and multihoming do nothing about two devices fighting over one address.

choices: Set the server NIC and the switch port to auto-negotiate (or both to 1 Gbps full duplex) and verify the error counters stop climbing
Replace the file server's hard drives with faster models
Enable jumbo frames on the workstations only
Install a second NIC in the server and team them for more bandwidth
desc: Find a duplex mismatch crushing file-server throughput.
hint: One end says half duplex, the other says full — and the collision counters are enormous. Ethernet collisions should be near zero on a modern full-duplex link.
objectives: Compare negotiated speed and duplex on both ends of the link
Check switch port error counters
Align autonegotiation settings
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: File copies to the department file server crawl at about 10 MB/s even though both the server and the workstations have gigabit NICs and the switch ports are gigabit-capable. Small files feel fine; large transfers and backups are painfully slow.
title: Gigabit Network, Megabit Speeds
why: The server NIC is at 100 Mbps half duplex while the other side is full duplex — a classic duplex mismatch, which generates exactly these collision and FCS error storms and crushes throughput. Aligning autonegotiation on both ends fixes the root cause. Faster disks, one-sided jumbo frames, or NIC teaming cannot fix a layer-1/2 mismatch.

choices: Unlock the account, then update or remove the saved old password on LT-RIOS-OLD (Wi-Fi profile and any cached credentials)
Unlock the account and tell her to wait an hour before logging in again
Reset her password again to something simpler she can type reliably
Disable the account lockout policy so this stops happening
desc: Trace repeated AD lockouts to a stale credential on an old device.
evidence:
A user account was locked out.
Target Account Name: m.rios
Caller Computer Name: LT-RIOS-OLD
Her previous laptop, still powered on in a drawer, with the corporate Wi-Fi profile saved under the old password.
hint: The 4740 event names the caller computer — the bad attempts are not coming from the machine in front of her.
objectives: Confirm the lockout state and frequency
Trace the lockout source in the domain controller security log
Eliminate the stale credential
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A user changed her password this morning and has been locked out of her domain account four times since. The helpdesk unlocks it, and within twenty minutes it locks again. She insists she is typing the new password correctly.
title: The Account That Keeps Locking
why: Event 4740 shows the lockout source is her old laptop LT-RIOS-OLD, which keeps authenticating with the pre-change password from saved Wi-Fi and cached credentials. Unlocking alone just restarts the twenty-minute cycle. Removing the stale credential on the source device ends it. Waiting, re-resetting, or weakening the lockout policy treats symptoms or creates risk.

choices: Have the firewall team re-allow RPC (TCP 135 plus the dynamic RPC port range) from the main-site DCs to BR-DC01, then force replication and re-check
Demote and re-promote BR-DC01
Manually copy the password hashes between domain controllers
Restart the main-site domain controller
desc: Restore AD replication blocked by a firewall change (error 1722).
evidence:
Source DSA: HQ-DC02 ... Destination DSA: BR-DC01
12 consecutive failures since 2026-10-03 02:14
Last error: 1722 (0x6ba): The RPC server is unavailable.
hint: DNS resolves fine, but TCP 135 does not answer — this is a connectivity block, not a broken directory.
objectives: Check replication health with repadmin
Verify name resolution and RPC connectivity to the partner DC
Identify the blocking point
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: Password changes made at the main site are not reaching the branch domain controller, and vice versa. Users at the branch sometimes cannot log on with new passwords. The problem started after weekend firewall maintenance at the branch.
title: Branch DC Stops Replicating
why: Error 1722 with DNS resolving but port 135 unreachable points squarely at the firewall change blocking RPC endpoint-mapper traffic to BR-DC01 — and AD replication needs the dynamic RPC range too. Restoring the firewall rules fixes replication without touching the directory. Demotion, manual hash copying, or rebooting the healthy DC are drastic, unsupported, or irrelevant.

choices: Have her log off and log back on to build a fresh logon token, then retry the share
Add her to the group again in case the first attempt did not save
Grant her user account direct read permission on the share instead
Restart the file server
desc: Explain why new group membership needs a fresh logon token.
evidence:
GROUP INFORMATION
-----------------
... Finance-Reports is NOT listed ...
hint: She is in the group in AD, but her logon token was built before she was added — Windows checks the token, not live group membership, for share access.
objectives: Verify the user is actually a group member
Check the groups in the user's current logon token
Trigger a token refresh
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A technician added a user to the Finance-Reports security group an hour ago so she could open a restricted share, but she still gets 'Access is denied'. The technician verified the group grants the share read permission and that the change replicated.
title: Added to the Group, Still Denied
why: Group membership takes effect in the access token created at logon; whoami /groups proves her current token predates the change. A fresh logon rebuilds the token with the new group. Re-adding her, granting direct permissions, or rebooting the server ignore how Windows authorization actually works.

choices: Launch PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass scoped to that one process and run the script: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\New-HireSetup.ps1
Run Set-ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Force so scripts always run on this machine
Open an elevated PowerShell prompt and run the script again
Rename the script to New-HireSetup.bat so the policy does not apply
desc: Run a trusted unsigned script without permanently weakening execution policy.
evidence:
.\New-HireSetup.ps1 : File C:\Scripts\New-HireSetup.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system. For more information, see about_Execution_Policies.
    + CategoryInfo          : SecurityError: (:) [], PSSecurityException

MachinePolicy : Undefined
UserPolicy    : Undefined
Process       : Undefined
CurrentUser   : Undefined
LocalMachine  : Undefined   (effective: Restricted)
The script is unsigned; it was copied from the team's file share this morning.
hint: Elevation does not change the policy, and the goal is to run this one trusted script — not to permanently lower the machine's defenses.
objectives: Read the exact error text
Check the effective execution policy
Run the script without permanently weakening the machine's policy
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A junior admin tries to run the team's standard onboarding script, .\New-HireSetup.ps1, on a fresh workstation and gets a red error. The same script runs fine on older machines. Nothing about the script itself changed.
title: Scripts Are Disabled on This System
why: The error is an execution-policy block (effective Restricted), not a permissions problem, so elevation changes nothing and renaming the file is evasion, not a fix. A process-scoped Bypass runs this one trusted script without permanently weakening the machine; Unrestricted would leave every future script — malicious or not — free to run.

choices: Switch to -LDAPFilter with the value embedded directly: Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter "(name=*O'Brien*)"
Double the apostrophe inside the -Filter string: "Name -like '*O''Brien*'"
Strip apostrophes from the search term before querying
Pipe all users to Where-Object instead: Get-ADUser -Filter * | Where-Object {$_.Name -like "*O'Brien*"}
desc: Fix an AD filter parsing failure on names containing apostrophes.
evidence: Get-ADUser : Error parsing query: 'Name -like '*O'Brien*'' Error Message: 'syntax error' at position 16
hint: The -Filter language has its own quoting rules that break on embedded quotes; LDAP filters do not share that parser.
objectives: Reproduce the parsing failure
Understand why the AD filter parser chokes on the apostrophe
Rewrite the query with an LDAP filter
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: An admin's user-lookup script works for every name except ones containing an apostrophe. Searching for 'O'Brien' throws a parsing error, while 'Smith' returns instantly. The script builds the filter by embedding the search term in double quotes.
title: The Apostrophe That Broke the Filter
why: The AD -Filter parser interprets the apostrophe as a string terminator, so no amount of doubling fixes it inside -Filter syntax. An -LDAPFilter passes the value straight to the directory, where apostrophes are legal in the attribute value. Stripping characters corrupts the search, and pulling every user object to filter client-side is a performance disaster at scale.

choices: Add PRINT-SRV to the client's TrustedHosts list and verify Enable-PSRemoting has been run on PRINT-SRV, then retry
Disable the Windows Firewall on both machines
Create a local account on PRINT-SRV with the same username and password as the admin's account
Run Enter-PSSession with -Authentication Basic over HTTP
desc: Resolve a WinRM TrustedHosts failure remoting to a workgroup server.
evidence:
Enter-PSSession : Connecting to remote server PRINT-SRV failed with the following error message : The WinRM client cannot process the request. ... Add the destination computer to the TrustedHosts list ...
    + CategoryInfo          : OpenError: (PRINT-SRV:String) [], PSRemotingTransportException
hint: The error names the exact missing piece — the client does not trust the destination. Test-WSMan proves the service itself is up.
objectives: Read the WinRM error precisely
Distinguish authentication failure from transport/trust failure
Configure the client trust entry and confirm remoting is enabled on the target
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: An admin tries Enter-PSSession -ComputerName PRINT-SRV from her workstation to restart the spooler remotely, but the connection is refused before credentials are even accepted. Both machines are in the same workgroup; there is no domain.
title: WinRM Will Not Trust the Server
why: In a workgroup, Kerberos mutual authentication is unavailable, so the WinRM client requires the target in TrustedHosts — the error says exactly that, and Test-WSMan confirms the service is listening. Mirrored local accounts, firewall-off, or Basic-over-HTTP either miss the actual block or trade it for cleartext credentials.

choices: Export the {8F3B2A1C-...} uninstall key as a backup, delete the key, then rerun the installer
Manually recreate the missing program files folder so the versions match
Install an even newer version number to satisfy the version check
Edit the DisplayVersion value down to 0.0.0 and leave the key in place
desc: Clear a stale Uninstall registry key blocking a fresh install.
evidence: FindRelatedProducts: found related product {8F3B2A1C-...}, version 5.4.0 - aborting: a newer version is already installed.
C:\Program Files\Contoso VPN - folder does not exist
hint: The installer trusts the registry, not the filesystem — a leftover registration from a botched uninstall is lying to it.
objectives: Locate the stale product registration
Back up the registry key before changing it
Remove the orphaned entry and retry the install
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: An engineer tries to install the current release of the company's VPN client, but the installer aborts with 'A newer version of this product is already installed.' Programs and Features shows no VPN client at all, and the program files folder is empty.
title: The Ghost of an Uninstall Past
why: FindRelatedProducts reads the Uninstall key, and the orphaned key (files long gone) is what blocks setup. Exporting then deleting the stale key removes the false positive while keeping a rollback copy. Recreating folders, inflating versions, or fudging DisplayVersion leaves a corrupt registration that will break future upgrades and uninstalls.

choices: Confirm with the security team that no USB block is intended; then back up the key, set Start to 3 (Manual), and replug the drive
Set Start to 1 (System start) so USB storage is always loaded at boot
Reinstall Windows to restore the default driver configuration
Buy a new flash drive - this one is probably failing
desc: Restore USB storage blocked by a disabled USBSTOR service key.
evidence: Same query on a working PC
hint: Start=4 means Disabled; Start=3 is the normal Manual setting. But first make sure nobody blocked USB on purpose.
objectives: Compare behavior across machines to isolate the fault
Inspect the USB storage driver start type
Restore the driver after ruling out a deliberate policy block
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A user's USB flash drive is not recognized on her workstation — no drive letter, no Device Manager entry — yet the same drive works on every other PC in the office. Nothing was recently installed.
title: USB Drive Works Everywhere but Here
why: USBSTOR at Start 4 (Disabled) explains why the drive works everywhere else and why no GPO is involved — likely a leftover manual tweak. Setting it back to 3 (Manual) restores normal plug-and-play after confirming the block was not a deliberate security control. Start=1 is wrong for a PnP driver, reinstalling Windows is wildly disproportionate, and the drive is proven good.

choices: Boot into Safe Mode, export the ArcPack ContextMenuHandlers key as backup, delete it, reboot normally, and confirm right-click works
Uninstall and reinstall the archiving utility with default options
Run SFC /scannow to repair explorer.exe
Create a new Windows user profile for the affected user
desc: Disable a crashing Explorer context-menu shell extension.
evidence:
Faulting application name: explorer.exe, version 10.0.22621.1
Faulting module name: ArcShell64.dll
Exception code: 0xc0000005
File-archiving utility 'ArcPack' - adds right-click menu entries.
hint: The crash only happens on right-click, and the faulting module belongs to the archiver's shell extension — remove the hook, not the whole program.
objectives: Identify the faulting module in the crash event
Boot to Safe Mode to break the crash loop
Disable the offending context-menu handler
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: Every time the user right-clicks a file, Explorer freezes and restarts. Left-click navigation works fine, and the problem started right after installing a file-archiving utility yesterday.
title: Right-Click Restarts Explorer
why: Event 1000 fingers ArcShell64.dll, the archiver's context-menu handler, as the crash module; right-click is exactly when that handler loads. Disabling its registry hook in Safe Mode (with an export as rollback) surgically removes the fault. Reinstalling the same extension reintroduces it, SFC cannot fix a third-party DLL, and a new profile dodges rather than fixes the machine-wide handler.

choices: Archive or truncate /var/log/myapp/app.log, fix the application's debug-level logging, and configure logrotate for it
Delete everything under /var/log to free space quickly
Extend the /var partition immediately - the disk is simply too small
Reboot the server to release the disk space
desc: Recover a full /var filesystem caused by a runaway log file.
evidence:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        50G   50G     0 100% /var
hint: One 44 GB log file is the entire problem — deleting logs blindly destroys evidence, and a reboot will not shrink a file.
objectives: Identify which filesystem is full
Find what is consuming the space
Clear space safely and prevent recurrence
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A web application starts throwing write errors, and users cannot upload files. The server has plenty of RAM and CPU free, and the database is healthy.
title: Disk Full: The 44 GB Log File
why: A single runaway log at debug verbosity consumed /var; truncating or archiving it restores service immediately, and logrotate plus a sane log level stops the recurrence. Wiping /var/log destroys audit evidence, extending the disk just postpones the same failure, and rebooting does not free space held by an existing file.

choices: Decide which server should own port 80 per the migration plan; stop and disable the other (or move it to a different port), then start nginx
Change nginx to listen on port 8080 and tell users the new port
Kill PID 1187 and start nginx
Reinstall nginx to fix the broken bind
desc: Resolve two web servers contending for port 80.
evidence:
Active: failed (Result: exit-code)
Oct 03 08:02 nginx[1120]: nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)
hint: Two web servers are both enabled and both want port 80 — killing one process does not survive a reboot.
objectives: Read the service failure output
Identify the process holding port 80
Resolve the conflict per the intended design
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: After a server migration, nginx fails to start on boot. The migration checklist says nginx should be the web server on this host, but something else is already answering on port 80.
title: Port 80 Is Already Taken
why: Both apache2 and nginx are enabled and contend for port 80; the fix is a design decision (which server serves this host) followed by disabling the loser so the conflict cannot return after reboot. Just killing the PID is temporary, moving nginx to 8080 contradicts the migration plan, and reinstalling nginx cannot fix another process holding the port.

choices: Set ~/.ssh to 700, authorized_keys to 600, the private key to 600, and ensure she owns all of them - then retry
Re-enable password authentication on the server so she can log in
Generate a brand-new key pair and register it with the server admin
Copy the keys to /tmp and SSH with -i /tmp/id_rsa
desc: Fix SSH key authentication refused due to unsafe file permissions.
evidence:
drwxrwxrwx 2 arao arao 4096 Oct  3 08:40 .ssh
-rwxrwxrwx 1 arao arao  394 Oct  3 08:40 authorized_keys
-rwxrwxrwx 1 arao arao 1679 Oct  3 08:40 id_rsa
journalctl -u sshd --since '1 hour ago' | grep -i refus
Oct 03 08:55:12 srv-web01 sshd[2241]: Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/arao/.ssh

debug1: Offering public key: id_rsa RSA SHA256:...
debug1: Server refused our key
hint: sshd is telling you exactly what is wrong: the modes. OpenSSH refuses keys when the files are group/world-writable.
objectives: Check the client and server-side key file permissions
Read the server's authentication refusal reason
Restore the required ownership and modes
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: An engineer restored her home directory from backup onto a new workstation and can no longer SSH with her key — she is prompted for a password, which she does not have on the remote server. Password SSH was already disabled there.
title: Server Refused Our Key
why: The restore preserved data but not safe modes — 777 on .ssh and the key files makes sshd refuse key auth by design. Restoring 700/600 with correct ownership satisfies StrictModes. Re-enabling passwords weakens the server, a new key pair is unnecessary work, and /tmp keys inherit worse problems.

choices: Reclassify to P4 per the matrix, apologize to the on-call engineer, and route the ticket to the web content queue
Keep P1 - the reporter is a department head, so it deserves critical handling
Close the ticket as 'not an IT issue' since it is just a typo
Escalate to P1 confirmed and assign a developer immediately
desc: Correct a mis-prioritized ticket using the impact/urgency matrix.
evidence:
Priority: P1 - Critical
Impact:   Single user (reporter)
Urgency:  Low - cosmetic, page fully usable
Service:  Intranet (operational)

P1: high impact + high urgency (service down, many users)
P4: low impact + low urgency (cosmetic, single user)
No SLA breach risk at P4; paged on-call engineer acknowledged, no action taken.
hint: Priority comes from impact x urgency in the matrix — not from who reported it or how loudly.
objectives: Apply the impact/urgency priority matrix
Reclassify the ticket correctly
Route it to the right queue without losing the report
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A level-1 technician logged a P1 (critical) ticket: 'Typo on the intranet homepage — says "recieve" instead of "receive".' The on-call engineer was paged at 6 AM. The service desk manager asks you to review whether the priority is correct.
title: A P1 Typo
why: The matrix is explicit: single-user cosmetic issues with no service degradation are P4, and paging on-call for a typo burns goodwill and budget. Reporter seniority does not change impact/urgency math, closing it loses a legitimate fix, and escalating doubles down on the original error.

choices: Log an emergency change record, get the duty manager's approval, implement the rule correction, and book the retrospective CAB review
Implement the fix now and file the change record tomorrow morning when the change manager is in
Wait for the next scheduled CAB - policy is policy
Ask the on-call engineer to make the change quietly and mention it at the next CAB
desc: Handle an outage fix through the emergency change process.
evidence: Emergency change: required to restore a degraded or critical service; needs approval from the emergency change approver (duty manager); must be logged before implementation; retrospective CAB review within 2 business days.
INC-48210, P1, payment portal unreachable since 14:20; root cause: firewall rule FW-2214 too restrictive.
hint: The policy already anticipated exactly this scenario — emergency changes exist so outages do not wait five days, but they still need a record and an approver.
objectives: Classify the change correctly under the change policy
Obtain the required emergency approval
Implement, document, and schedule retrospective review
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: At 9 PM the monitoring system pages: the payment portal is down because a firewall rule change this afternoon blocked its traffic. The fix is a one-line rule correction, but the CAB meets weekly and the next window is five days away. Revenue is being lost every hour.
title: Outage at 9 PM, CAB in Five Days
why: The outage qualifies as an emergency change: restore service now with duty-manager approval, a record logged before implementation, and a retrospective review. Implementing without a record or quietly bypasses the audit trail; waiting five days for CAB while revenue burns misreads the policy's intent.

choices: Escalate to the queue manager now, reassign to an available engineer, and post a status update to the sales team acknowledging the delay
Wait - the SLA has not breached yet, so no action is required
Close the ticket and ask the sales team to open a new one on Monday
Change the priority to P4 to stop the SLA clock
desc: Escalate an at-risk ticket with a silent, absent assignee.
evidence: Opened 06:12 (P2, SLA 8h) -> triaged 06:40 -> last update 07:05 ('looking into it') -> now 13:00, no updates.
Out of office until Monday; ticket still assigned to them.
hint: An SLA at 85% with a silent, absent assignee is exactly what escalation paths are for — waiting for the breach is a choice to breach.
objectives: Recognize the SLA risk and the communication gap
Escalate through the proper path
Restore customer confidence with a status update
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A P2 ticket ('VPN intermittent for the sales team') is at 85% of its 8-hour SLA, has had no update in six hours, and the assignee went on leave without reassigning it. The sales team is asking for status in the ticket thread.
title: SLA at 85 Percent, Nobody Home
why: Escalation exists to intervene before breach: the queue manager can reassign to someone present, and a status update repairs the six-hour silence. Waiting guarantees a breach, closing and re-opening is ticket fraud, and downgrading priority to stop the clock falsifies the record.

choices: Power off and unplug, reseat the RAM modules, then test booting with one stick at a time to isolate a bad module or slot
Replace the power supply - beeps mean it is failing
Flash the BIOS to the latest version
Replace the CMOS battery
desc: Diagnose a no-POST beep pattern after the PC was moved.
evidence: Power on -> fans spin -> repeating long beeps -> no video output -> never reaches the vendor logo screen.
PC was transported to a different desk this morning.
Monitor and cable verified good on another PC.
hint: Repeating beeps with no video after the machine was physically moved screams 'something unseated in transit' — and memory is the usual suspect.
objectives: Interpret the no-POST symptom pattern
Isolate the faulty component safely
Confirm the fix with a minimal boot test
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A desktop powers on — fans spin, lights come on — but there is no display, and it emits a repeating pattern of long beeps. It never reaches the vendor logo. The machine worked fine yesterday and was moved to a different desk this morning.
title: Beeps, No Display, After a Move
why: Repeating beeps with no POST and no video is the classic memory-detection failure, and transport commonly unseats RAM. Reseating and single-stick testing isolates a bad module or slot with zero cost. The PSU is delivering power (fans spin), a BIOS flash on a non-POSTing board is risky and unwarranted, and the CMOS battery cannot cause beep-code POST failures.

choices: Back up the data immediately (image or file copy), minimize further drive use, then replace the drive and restore
Run a full chkdsk /r to repair the bad sectors first
Defragment the drive to improve performance
Update the storage drivers - the caution status is probably a software misreport
desc: Respond to rising SMART reallocated-sector counts on a failing drive.
evidence:
Health Status: Caution
Reallocated Sectors Count: 184 (rising over the last week)
Current Pending Sector Count: 24
Intermittent 20-30 second freezes; one blue-screen crash yesterday.
No backup configured; roughly 340 GB of local project data.
hint: Rising reallocated and pending sectors mean the drive is physically dying — every extra read/write risks the data. Back up first, diagnose later.
objectives: Read the SMART indicators correctly
Prioritize data preservation over further diagnostics
Plan the drive replacement
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A user's workstation occasionally freezes for 20-30 seconds, and the drive health tool now shows a 'Caution' status. The user has years of local project files with no backup. Yesterday the machine blue-screened once.
title: SMART Says Caution
why: Reallocated and pending sector counts climbing together signal physical media failure in progress; the only safe first move is getting the irreplaceable data off before the drive degrades further. chkdsk /r hammers a dying drive with writes and can precipitate total failure, defrag is pointless wear, and drivers do not cause SMART reallocations.

choices: Power down, clean the dust from heatsinks and fans, verify or replace the dead case fan, check the CPU cooler mount, and re-test under load
Increase the Windows page file to reduce CPU strain
Undervolt the CPU in the BIOS to lower temperatures
Replace the power supply - sudden shutdowns are always the PSU
desc: Fix thermal shutdowns caused by dust-blocked cooling.
evidence:
CPU package: 97 C -> 99 C -> (shutdown)
Fan: 100% for 12 minutes before shutdown.
Heatsink fins packed with dust; one case fan not spinning.
Event 41, Kernel-Power: 'The system has rebooted without cleanly shutting down first.'
hint: 97-99 C with a dead fan and dust-packed heatsink is thermal protection doing its job — fix the cooling, not the power or the page file.
objectives: Correlate shutdowns with thermal data
Inspect cooling hardware
Restore normal thermals and verify under load
prompt: What is the best next action?
situation: A CAD workstation shuts off without warning during rendering jobs, then powers back on fine. Event logs show no software crash — just an unexpected shutdown. The tower sits in a dusty corner and its fans sound like a jet engine under load.
title: Shutdowns Under Load
why: The sensor log shows the CPU hitting its thermal limit before each shutdown — the firmware's protection mechanism, confirmed by dust blockage and a dead fan. Cleaning, restoring airflow, and checking the cooler mount address the actual cause. The page file is irrelevant to thermals, undervolting masks the cooling failure, and the PSU is innocent when temperatures explain the shutdowns.
